 How youth voters at Contra Costa College navigated Election Day
 Contra Costa College hosted many first-time voters this rainy Election Day, who turned out primarily in support of public transit 
 By Rachel Burnett , Richmond Confidential Staff 
 • 
 Nov 17, 2026 
 Rachel Burnett The Contra Costa College Library holds a voting information display at the entrance on November 3. 
 Youth voters at Contra Costa College moved anxiously across campus this rainy Election Day, as they navigated the voting process and awaited results of a regional measure that would support public transit.
 “I’m excited to vote and start getting into the political process,” said Hepsy Cerrato, 18 year old CCC student and first-time voter.
 Cerrato was registered before her 18th birthday and worked as an election poll worker in the 2026 Primary Election.
 Contra Costa College — with 5,980 students between the ages of 18-24 — worked to prepare voters like Cerrato for Tuesday’s election by providing resources and holding events across campus. Contra Costa County has 83,389 registered voters between the ages of 17.5 and 25, making up approximately 11.38% of total registered voters.
 Story continues below advertisement 
 Students interviewed on campus Tuesday said they were experiencing a range of emotions, from enthusiasm to dread.
 “In a way, there’s a stigma of the youth not caring,” said student Jasmine Sanchez, 19. “Use your voice for the betterment and empowerment of your people and community… You’re making an impact, and I think that should be emphasized.”
 The Regional Transit Measure (RTM), an ambitious, five-county sales tax measure, was top of mind amongst students who rely on public transportation. If passed, the 0.5% sales tax would generate revenue for regional public transit services, including BART, which was facing drastic service cuts without the money.
 “My dad works for BART, so he has a possibility of losing his job if they aren’t getting enough votes,” she said. “I really hope BART is saved.”
 Student and first-time voter Aaliyah Mariah Zanod, 18, said the transit measure was important to her and her family as she proudly showed off her ‘I Voted’ sticker.
 The official ballot box at Contra Costa College remains quiet as the rain persists on Election Day, 2026. 
 Learning how to navigate the voting process, locate ballot drop-off boxes and find information about the races and measures was new for many first-time voters on campus. Senior Library Technician Joe Roberts said he helped about 10 students before 1 p.m.
 The library staff also created an online ‘Vote 2026’ guide that included resources for voter registration, ballot information, and where to submit ballots.
 “Our librarians take very good care of being able to help people,” Roberts said. “This is the one place that they know, no matter what, they can get information.”
 The Student and Administration Building is in view on November 3, 2026 as students rush to class on the rainy Election Day. (Rachel Burnett) 
 The Associated Students Union also hosted a ‘What’s on my ballot’ forum on October 15 with Contra Costa College District governing board candidates and information about the election. Student Union Vice President Steve Sandoval said engagement was high as they had to limit the amount of student questions during the candidate Q&A.
 “Being informed is one of the best things that you can be,” Sandoval said.
 Student Julissa Blandon, 19, had her ballot in hand while she grabbed lunch and planned to submit it at the ballot box on campus. “For a lot of students, especially on campus, they have Cal Fresh, or they have Medi-Cal or FAFSA,” she said. “All these things matter, and they’re on the ballot.”
 Blandon canvassed for Richmond Mayor candidate Claudia Jimenez, who was officially elected on Nov. 6.
 “Your vote matters,” Blandon said. “In your own story and your own family, in some way, it’s affecting you.”
